title: Ohio elects Amy Acton first woman governor
body:
Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Dr. Amy Acton speaks to media outside her polling place on the Capitol University campus after voting in Columbus, Ohio, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
                
                    Carolyn Kaster/AP Photo
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Carolyn Kaster/AP Photo
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Democrat Amy Acton, Ohio's former health director, will be the state's next governor, according to a race call by The Associated Press.   She is the first woman elected governor of Ohio.   Acton beat out biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican backed by President Trump, in a race defined in the final weeks by mudslinging and a Ramaswamy attack ad that drew national criticism, including from some Republicans.   Her win marks the first time in two decades that Ohioans have elected a Democrat to lead the state.   
    Loading... 
   Outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine made Acton, 60, the Ohio Department of Health director early in his first term. During the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, the two held regular briefings together, where they announced lockdowns and promoted safety measures, until Acton's resignation from the post in June 2020.   During the campaign, Acton highlighted her background in public health, not politics, and embraced policies like a statewide child tax credit and medical debt forgiveness.   Late in October, the race for governor garnered national attention when the Ramaswamy campaign flooded airwaves with an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calling Acton a "liar." Arthur lost custody of Acton when she was 12 over the alleged sexual assault of Acton by Arthur's husband, Acton's stepfather.   The ad faced blowback from Republicans, including DeWine, but Trump and Ramaswamy defended it.   Democrats in Ohio have endured bruising elections statewide the last few cycles. Acton will take office in January with a GOP-majority legislature that's likely to severely limit her authority.   Sarah Donaldson covers politics and government for the Ohio Public Radio and Television Statehouse News Bureau.

title: 5 DSA candidates are elected to the House in a historic night for their movement
body:
Congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier speaks at a rally at King's Theater on June 18, 2026 in New York City. She is among a slate of DSA-backed candidates heading to Congress after midterm election victories.
                
                    Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      In a historic night for the Democratic Socialists of America, a record number of candidates endorsed by the organization and its local chapters were elected to the House of Representatives.   The results grow the organization's presence on Capitol Hill, bringing to Congress a bloc of lawmakers who will now look to translate their electoral success into policy wins that push the Democratic Party further to the left.   At least five DSA candidates in reliably blue congressional districts have won their races, according to race calls by the Associated Press. They are Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York; Melat Kiros in Colorado; Donavan McKinney in Michigan; and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania.   
   Their victories follow a fiercely competitive primary cycle, where DSA candidates rode to victory by championing economic populist policies like universal healthcare and childcare, as well as more polarizing stances, such as abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.   Throughout the primaries, candidates endorsed by the group were unafraid to criticize or break with Democratic leadership, challenging sitting incumbents or competing against establishment picks.   That included Kiros, who defeated Rep. Diana DeGette — a 15-term incumbent and member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus — in Colorado's 1st Congressional District in July. Just days earlier, Chevalier delivered a major upset in New York's 13th Congressional District, narrowly defeating Adriano Espaillat, the influential chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.   On top of emphasizing a core value set aimed at bettering the working class, many DSA candidates tapped into voter frustrations with the larger political system. Candidates swore off campaign donations from corporations and pro-Israel lobbying groups. They fiercely condemned the war in Gaza and called for the U.S. to stop supplying Israel with military aid.   While the DSA's platform energized some voters on the left, it also became a prominent attack line for Republicans, who sought to paint the broader Democratic Party as too extreme and link more moderate candidates to democratic socialist figures like New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.   
   The DSA is not a registered political party, but with Tuesday's victories, the number of DSA members in the House is on track to more than triple when the new Congress is seated in January. Currently just two sitting lawmakers — Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Ocasio-Cortez — are members of the organization.   It's a small, albeit growing coalition, but one that could complicate the legislative agenda of Democrats if they succeed in winning back the House. In a new Congress where Democrats have only a thin majority, the bloc could wield outsize influence. If Democrats can win a broader majority, their influence could prove more limited.   The upcoming vote for House speaker may serve as an early test. If Democrats win the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is poised to be elected the nation's first Black speaker. Currently, none of the incoming members with DSA endorsements has committed to supporting Jeffries.    Loading...

title: Tens of millions cast ballots for midterms despite worries of Trump's interference
description: People wait in line to vote Tuesday at C
body:
People wait in line to vote Tuesday at Canfield Community Center in Dearborn Heights, Mich.
                
                    Salwan Georges/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Salwan Georges/Getty Images
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Tens of millions of voters cast their ballots Tuesday without widespread disruptions despite concerns of interference by the Trump administration.   Around the country, election administrators responded to relatively common Election Day issues in some communities, from delayed poll openings and long lines to poor signage and voting equipment problems.    Polls remain open in much of the western United States until later Tuesday.   Flooding in parts of Florida and in the Four Corners states of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah forced local officials to relocate some polling sites and resort to emergency ballots.   
   The most high-profile technical problem occurred in Westchester County, N.Y., which includes part of the state's competitive 17th Congressional District. A ballot scanner issue took much of the day to get sorted out, meaning voters had to give their ballots to election workers for scanning at a later time. Some right-wing commentators online claimed the issue was a sign of fraud, but both the Republican and Democrat running in the district told voters not to be deterred.   "Every ballot will be counted," Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent in the district, wrote in an X post after news of the issue arose.   The Trump administration's Justice Department had announced it planned to have around 1,000 monitors at polling places on Election Day, and shortly after the first polls opened on the East Coast Tuesday, the department said it was sending monitors to observe voting in every state.   "Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division," Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said in a statement.   
   Sending out election observers has been a routine way of documenting any racial discrimination at the polls under past administrations since the passing of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But ongoing, baseless claims of widespread voter fraud from President Trump and other federal officials had heightened worries among many local officials and election experts that this administration's DOJ election monitors would interfere with voting at the polls.   As of Tuesday evening, however, no such activity has been reported.   But the New Mexico secretary of state's office received reports of DOJ monitors asking unusual questions and questioning voters in Bernalillo County, which is home to Albuquerque. "The New Mexico Department of Justice reached out to the DOJ Team Lead on our office's behalf to address this reported behavior, and we received assurances it would be addressed," spokesperson Lindsey Bachman said in a statement.   
   Concerns about Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and law enforcement presence near polling sites also did not come to pass, as of 9 p.m. ET.   Instead, voters exercised their rights on what many voting observers considered to be a fairly normal Election Day.   Their ballots on Tuesday joined more than 61 million that were already cast during early voting. Nationally, early in-person and mail-in voters cast 34% more ballots compared to the last midterm general elections in 2022, according to the latest data compiled by the University of Florida's Election Lab. The pre-Election Day surge was driven mainly by in-person voting.   As the counting of ballots continues, voting rights advocates are now looking ahead to any potential controversies over close races and the certification of results. Some election officials have also warned about ballot seizures, especially after the FBI earlier this year seized election 2020 materials from Fulton County, Ga.   "Election Day is the last day that you can cast your ballot. But election season continues after today, and we're going to continue to remain vigilant," said Shaylyn Cochran, deputy executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, during a press call on Tuesday.   Edited by Benjamin Swasey

title: Democrat Sherrod Brown wins Ohio Senate race
body:
Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) speaks during a campaign rally with former President Barack Obama at the Cleveland Public Auditorium on Oct. 24, 2026.
                
                    Jeff Swensen/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jeff Swensen/Getty Images
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Democratic former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown has won back a seat on Capitol Hill, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted after a close and expensive battle, according to a race call by the Associated Press.   Brown is the seventh former U.S. senator since 1946 to lose his seat and then return to the Senate later.   
    Loading... 
   After serving three terms, he was defeated by Bernie Moreno in 2024 in what the ad tracking site AdImpact ranked as the most expensive non-presidential election on record at the time (that honor now goes to this year's Senate race in Texas).   This was Husted's first race for the U.S. Senate. He was appointed to the seat by Gov. Mike DeWine in January 2023 after JD Vance won the vice presidency. But Husted has had a long career in elected office in Ohio, serving as speaker of the Ohio House, the secretary of state and lieutenant governor.   Ohio has been a Republican stronghold for years, with President Trump winning Ohio in the last three presidential cycles. But because of Brown's name recognition, polls showed the race was close all year, and it got more attention amid building signs of a national "blue wave" for Democrats.   The campaign started quietly, with neither Brown nor Husted doing a splashy launch. Both leaned toward smaller events at first, but joined big rallies that came up in the last month.    Loading... 
   Brown was part of a rally led by former President Barack Obama on Oct. 24. And Husted met up with Trump in his three visits to Ohio in October, and became one of several male office-seekers who earned odd praise from Trump on their physiques.   
   Data centers, affordability, the war in Iran and health care costs were major issues in the campaign. Brown had made data centers a key talking point, calling Husted "the face of data centers" in Ohio because of his involvement with such deals when he was lieutenant governor. A leaked memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee defined data centers as "the anchor hanging around Husted's neck" and suggested if Husted lost, it would affect future races around the country. (NPR hasn't independently confirmed the authenticity of the memo.)   Brown far outraised Husted, with the candidates together bringing in more than $80 million. Ohio was the only state with a close U.S. Senate race where Democrats had more broadcast TV ads than Republicans, according to AdImpact. As of mid-October, the candidates and outside groups had spent more than $422 million, making this race one of the most expensive U.S. Senate contests in the country.   
   Brown is assured of only two more years in the U.S. Senate. Because this year's election was to fill the rest of the term Vance was elected to in 2022, Brown will have to run for reelection in 2028 to keep the seat.

title: Democrat Annie Andrews wins South Carolina Senate race in major upset
description: Dr. Annie Andrews answers questions from
body:
Dr. Annie Andrews answers questions from members of the media after greeting poll workers on Election Day at the Royal Missionary Baptist Church on Tuesday.
                
                    Win McNamee/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Win McNamee/Getty Images
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Democrat Annie Andrews has defeated GOP Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina's Senate race, according to a race call by the Associated Press.   Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman to win a Senate election in South Carolina, and the first Democratic Senator elected in the state since 1998. It's a stunning upset in a state that President Trump won by nearly 18 points in 2024, and a critical pickup for Democrats hoping to regain control of the Senate.   
    Loading... 
   Graham was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, longtime Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, in July. She was a key vote for Trump in recent months, fighting Democratic efforts to reign in Trump's war powers and confirming Todd Blanche as Attorney General.   However, she faced a tough political landscape for Republicans, as Trump's approval ratings hit record lows in the weeks before the midterms, driven largely by opposition to the war in Iran, the president's tariff policies and high energy prices.    Andrews made affordability issues central to her campaign, arguing that she would fight to end tax breaks for the wealthy, raise wages and push for affordable child care. She also drew on her career as a pediatrician, and said her experience treating patients who faced financial barriers to health care was a major factor that pushed her into politics.   "I would diagnose kids with common chronic diseases like asthma and diabetes, and I found that while I would explain my treatment plan to the parents so often, they would say, 'Well, how much is that inhaler going to cost?' Or 'How much is that insulin going to cost?'" Andrews told NPR in an interview last month. "No parent in America should have to be thinking about their pocketbook when they're hearing news that their child has a chronic illness."   
   The South Carolina race is key to Democrats' hopes to flip Senate control. Democrats need to net four seats to win the majority. A favorable political landscape boosted Democrats in battleground states like North Carolina — where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper won another key Senate race — and expanded the competitive map to include seats in redder states like South Carolina, Kansas and Texas.    Loading...

title: Missouri voters turn down a Republican-backed congressional map
description: Voters Antonia Loomis, left, and Carl Ja
body:
Voters Antonia Loomis, left, and Carl Jacobs fill out their ballots on Tuesday's Election Day in Clayton, Mo.
                
                    Jeff Roberson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jeff Roberson/AP
    

   
   Missouri voters have denied a Republican-backed congressional map that wound its way through the courts before ultimately ending up on the state's ballot. That's according to a race call by the Associated Press.    Loading... 
   GOP lawmakers in Missouri had passed the map last year to try to oust Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver by redrawing his Kansas City district. The goal was to pick up an additional House seat for Republicans.   The new district lines came amid a national mid-decade redistricting rush that was initiated by President Trump to try to boost his party ahead of the midterm elections.   Missouri's top court ruled that the Republican-backed map could not be in effect for the midterms, and instead voters would get to decide on it. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld that state court ruling.   Cleaver easily won reelection Tuesday, according to a race call by the Associated Press.   Missouri is not the only state deciding ballot measures relating to redistricting.   Maryland voters approved a constitutional amendment to change rules for congressional redistricting, allowing Democratic state leaders to redraw districts ahead of the 2028 election.   And Colorado voters are deciding a constitutional amendment that would ban congressional maps that purposefully favor one political party.

title: Democrat James Talarico wins Texas Senate seat
description: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico ad
body:
Texas Senate candidate James Talarico addresses supporters on primary election night in Austin, Texas.
                
                    Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has won the U.S. Senate race in Texas, according to a race call from the Associated Press. Talarico's victory breaks the Republican Party's three-decade monopoly on statewide offices in Texas.   Talarico defeated Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Trump, in one of the most closely watched and expensive races this year.   
    Loading... 
   Talarico's victory is a major blow for Republicans and Trump himself. Trump and his allies poured millions of dollars into the race, and Trump often attacked Talarico in campaign rallies across the U.S., using him as a national stand-in for Democrats.   Paxton becomes the first Republican to lose a Texas Senate seat since 1990's.   Paxton, who had never lost a race since winning election to the Texas House of Representatives in 2002, defeated incumbent U.S. Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff election to capture the Republican nomination. He was helped in securing that victory by a last-minute endorsement from Trump.    Loading... 
   But with the president's popularity having dipped underwater, Trump's support may have acted as a drag on Paxton. The attorney general had expressed concern about this after Trump campaigned for Paxton at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in September.   Talarico, a four-term state lawmaker from Austin, tied or led Paxton in most statewide polls starting in midsummer. He led Paxton by a wide margin in fundraising for most of this year, although conservative super PACs allied to the attorney general offset that advantage with heavy spending on advertising in the final two months of the campaign.   Talarico first rose to prominence in the state in 2018 by flipping a heavily Republican state House district, which had voted for Donald Trump for president two years earlier. A former San Antonio middle school teacher and a Presbyterian seminarian, Talarico focused his campaign on education and staunchly opposed efforts to inject religion into the public school system. He was one of the most vocal opponents of a law requiring the display of an explicitly Protestant translation of the Ten Commandments in all public school classrooms, which is now subject to multiple federal lawsuits.   
   Talarico garnered national attention through an interview on The Joe Rogan Experience podcast in July 2025, followed by a February 2026 interview for The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. CBS declined to broadcast the latter interview, apparently under pressure from the Trump administration through the Federal Communications Commission, but it subsequently went viral on YouTube. That not only built his national name recognition but also transformed him into a fundraising juggernaut.   Throughout the campaign, Paxton also battled negative perceptions of his record related to past scandals involving his alleged corruption in office — which, in 2023, led to his impeachment by the Texas House of Representatives, and of which he was subsequently acquitted by the Texas Senate — as well as his ongoing divorce from state Sen. Angela Paxton over his alleged marital infidelities.
